results.title: Expression and witness are both real
results.text: Your gift honours God in itself, because it reflects the creativity of the God whose image you bear, and it serves others. That same faithful work is also a witness: people see good works and glorify the Father (Matt 5:16). Many evangelical and Reformed teachers (Keller, Crouch, Stott) and Catholic and Orthodox traditions hold this integrated view. Keep both: do the work well and in love, and be ready to speak when asked.

results.title: Your work is service to your neighbour
results.text: Ordinary work is not second-class. Paul tells workers to serve 'as for the Lord' (Col 3:23-24), and Luther taught that God feeds and cares for the world through people's daily callings. You do not need to attach a sermon to a well-made table or a carefully kept account for it to please God. Release the guilt; offer the work with thanks.

results.title: Use the opportunities to speak
results.text: Your life and work have earned you trust; now let your words follow. Paul asks how people will believe without hearing (Rom 10:14-15), and Peter says to be ready to give a reason for your hope, with gentleness and respect (1 Pet 3:15). This is not a betrayal of good work but its natural partner. Evangelicals rightly insist that silence about Christ is not neutral.

results.title: Beware making people into projects
results.text: Love that is conditional on conversion is not yet the love Jesus showed. He healed ten lepers knowing nine would not return (Luke 17:11-19), and he looked at the rich young man and loved him though he walked away (Mark 10:21). Serve people because they bear God's image. Keep sharing Christ, but as a gift offered to a friend, not as a sale closed with a customer.

results.title: Gifts are for building up the body
results.text: Spirit gifts are given 'for the common good' (1 Cor 12:7) and to build up the church (1 Cor 14:12, Eph 4:12). Encouraging, teaching, helping and giving within the church are not lesser than evangelism; a loving, united church is itself a witness to the world (John 13:35, John 17:21).

results.title: Proclamation has a unique place
results.text: Some careful evangelical teachers (for example DeYoung and Gilbert, Piper) argue that because people face eternal judgement and salvation, the church's distinct mission is to proclaim Christ and make disciples. This is a serious view rooted in texts like Matt 28:18-20 and 2 Cor 5:20. Notice, though, that these same writers also affirm that a Christian's ordinary work and good deeds please God; they distinguish what the church as an institution is sent to do from everything a Christian may rightly do. Consider also the resurrection hope of a renewed creation (Rom 8:19-21).

results.title: Rest: your worth is not your output
results.text: If your gift has become a way to feel valuable, God's first answer is Sabbath. Even the holy work of the tabernacle stopped for rest (Exod 31:12-17). You are loved before you are useful. Receive that, then return to your gift with freedom rather than pressure.

timeline.title: How Christians have thought about gifts, work and witness

events.label: Bezalel builds the tabernacle
events.text: God fills Bezalel with his Spirit for skill in craft and gives Oholiab to help him (Exod 31:1-6). This is the traditional early date for the exodus; many scholars prefer about 1260 BC. Either way, Israel's memory puts artistic skill at the heart of worship.

events.label: David organises temple musicians
events.text: The Chronicler describes David appointing families of skilled singers and players, led by Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun, to 'prophesy' with instruments (1 Chr 25:1-7). Music becomes a permanent, trained ministry.

events.label: Christians in ordinary trades
events.text: The *Epistle to Diognetus* (second century, date uncertain) says Christians live in ordinary cities, follow local customs in dress and food, and yet show a remarkable way of life. Early Christians kept their trades, though writers like Tertullian (*On Idolatry*) said they must refuse work that served idol worship.

events.label: Benedict's Rule: prayer and work
events.text: The *Rule of St Benedict* (about 530) orders monastic life around set hours of prayer and set hours of manual work and reading; chapter 48 says idleness is the enemy of the soul. The famous motto 'ora et labora' (pray and work) summarises this rhythm, but the phrase itself is not in the Rule and seems to date from the nineteenth century.

events.label: Medieval ranking of callings
events.text: Abbot Suger dedicates the rebuilt choir of Saint-Denis near Paris, its light and coloured glass meant to lift the mind from material beauty to God. Medieval cathedrals were the work of thousands of skilled craftsmen, yet the 'religious' life of monks and clergy was ranked above lay work. This hierarchy goes back to writers like Eusebius of Caesarea (*Demonstration of the Gospel* 1.8, early fourth century), who described a 'perfect' life given wholly to God and a lower, 'permitted' life for those who farm, trade and marry.

events.label: Luther on calling
events.text: In his 1520 treatises Luther argues that all baptised Christians are priests and that the works of monks and priests are no holier in God's sight than the work of a farmer in the field or a woman in her household. Later he describes daily callings as 'masks of God' through which God cares for the world. The popular line about God 'milking the cows through the milkmaid' paraphrases this idea and is usually traced to Gustaf Wingren's summary, not to a confirmed Luther text.

events.label: Calvin's 'sentry post'
events.text: In the final edition of the *Institutes* (3.10.6), Calvin says God has assigned each person a calling, like a sentry post, so that no one drifts through life, and that no task is so humble that it does not shine before God when done in obedience.

events.label: Puritan teaching on calling
events.text: William Perkins's *A Treatise of the Vocations or Callings of Men* (published 1603) distinguishes a 'general calling' to be a Christian from a 'particular calling' to a trade, and teaches that both serve God and the common good. Later Puritans such as Richard Baxter developed this in detail.

events.label: Pietism and the heart
events.text: Philipp Jakob Spener's *Pia Desideria* calls for heart-religion, Bible study groups and active lay faith. Pietism energised missions, education and care for orphans (Francke at Halle), and also taught many to judge activities by their direct spiritual usefulness.

events.label: Bach: 'to God alone the glory'
events.text: J. S. Bach becomes cantor in Leipzig. He often headed scores 'J.J.' (Jesu juva, 'Jesus, help') and ended them 'S.D.G.' (Soli Deo gloria, 'to God alone the glory'), on secular pieces as well as church works. In his Bible he noted that 1 Chronicles 25 is the foundation of God-pleasing church music.

events.label: Wesley: 'The Use of Money'
events.text: John Wesley's sermon on money (preached from the 1740s and printed around 1760) urges Christians to gain all they can by honest work, save all they can and give all they can. Methodism joined fervent evangelism with schools, medicine and help for the poor.

events.label: Finney's 'new measures'
events.text: Charles Finney's *Lectures on Revivals of Religion* argue that revival is the right use of appropriate means, defending techniques such as the 'anxious bench'. Revivalism made the conversion of individuals the measure of the church's success, though Finney himself also backed abolition and social reform.

events.label: Moody and Sankey
events.text: D. L. Moody preaches and Ira Sankey sings across Britain (1873-1875). Sankey's gospel songs were written and sung to prepare hearers for the sermon. Moody famously described the world as a wrecked ship and his task as saving as many as he could in the lifeboat, an image that shaped generations of evangelical priorities.

events.label: Edinburgh Missionary Conference
events.text: The World Missionary Conference in Edinburgh, chaired by John R. Mott, gathers Protestant missions with the hope of evangelising the world 'in this generation'. Missions then included schools, hospitals and translation alongside preaching.

events.label: Fundamentalism and the 'great reversal'
events.text: After the Fundamentalist-Modernist controversies of the 1920s, many conservative Protestants withdrew from cultural and social engagement, which they linked with the liberal 'social gospel'. Historian Timothy L. Smith called this the 'great reversal', and sociologist David Moberg made the phrase famous in his 1972 book. Premillennial expectation of the end often reinforced the focus on saving souls.

events.label: Sayers: 'Why Work?'
events.text: In an address at Eastbourne on 23 April 1942, Dorothy L. Sayers argues that the church has failed workers by caring only that they are honest and come to church, not that their work is good. Work should be the full expression of a person's God-given faculties. Her book *The Mind of the Maker* (1941) links human creativity to the Trinity.

events.label: Billy Graham's crusades
events.text: Billy Graham's Los Angeles campaign launches decades of mass evangelism. Music, film, broadcasting and celebrity testimony were enlisted for the crusades, making 'using your gift for the gospel' a powerful and inspiring model for millions.

events.label: Jesus music becomes 'ministry'
events.text: Larry Norman's song 'Why Should the Devil Have All the Good Music?' (1972) captures the Jesus-music movement that grew into the Contemporary Christian Music industry. Debates followed for decades over whether Christian musicians were ministers who must mention Jesus or artists free to write about all of life.

events.label: Schaeffer: *Art and the Bible*
events.text: Francis Schaeffer argues that art is not justified only by being a vehicle for evangelism; a Christian's creativity is valuable as the work of a creature made in God's image. With his friend Hans Rookmaaker he encouraged evangelicals to take the arts seriously.

events.label: Lausanne Covenant
events.text: The International Congress on World Evangelization, led by Billy Graham and with John Stott as chief drafter of the Covenant, affirms that evangelism and socio-political involvement are both part of Christian duty, while stating that in the church's mission of sacrificial service evangelism is primary.

events.label: Crouch: *Culture Making*
events.text: Andy Crouch argues that the only way to change culture is to make more and better culture, and that Christians should move beyond condemning, critiquing, copying or consuming culture toward cultivating and creating it.

events.label: DeYoung and Gilbert
events.text: In *What Is the Mission of the Church?* Kevin DeYoung and Greg Gilbert argue that the church's distinct mission is to make disciples through proclaiming the gospel, while affirming that Christians should do good works and that ordinary vocations honour God. Their book is a careful counterweight to calls for 'holistic' mission.

events.label: Keller: *Every Good Endeavor*
events.text: Tim Keller, with Katherine Leary Alsdorf, presents work as part of God's good design, damaged by sin and redeemed through the gospel. The book draws on Luther and Sayers and helped spread the 'faith and work' movement. (Two years earlier, the Lausanne Cape Town Commitment of 2010 named the sacred-secular divide as a major obstacle to mission.)

events.label: Fujimura: *Culture Care*
events.text: Painter Makoto Fujimura calls Christians to 'culture care': tending culture like a garden, offering beauty as a gift rather than a weapon in culture wars. He develops this in *Art and Faith: A Theology of Making* (2020).

gallery.title: Gifts and talents: what they are, and how each can be expression and witness
gallery.intro: Filter by colour. Each card names a gift, shows where Scripture mentions it, gives people who show it, and describes how it can be both an expression of love and worship and a witness to Christ. The spiritual-gift lists are already in the Gifts section of the app; here the focus is on how each gift is used.

items.title: Prophecy
items.summary: Speaking a word from God that strengthens, encourages and comforts (1 Cor 14:3).
items.detail: Christians disagree on whether prophecy today means new revelation, Spirit-prompted insight, or faithful preaching. Expression: it is love speaking truth to build others up. Witness: Paul says an outsider who hears prophecy may be convicted and declare that God is truly among you (1 Cor 14:24-25).

items.title: Teaching
items.summary: Explaining God's word clearly so others understand and obey.
items.detail: Teachers carry extra responsibility (Jas 3:1). Expression: delight in truth and in other people's growth. Witness: clear teaching equips the whole church for its work in the world (Eph 4:12).

items.title: Encouragement (exhortation)
items.summary: Coming alongside people to urge, comfort and strengthen them.
items.detail: Barnabas' name means 'son of encouragement' (Acts 4:36). Expression: compassion in words. Witness: Barnabas vouched for Paul and saw grace in Antioch, and 'a great many people were added to the Lord' (Acts 11:23-24).

items.title: Giving
items.summary: Sharing resources generously and simply.
items.detail: Paul asks givers to give with generosity or simplicity (Rom 12:8) and cheerfully (2 Cor 9:7). Expression: joy in God's generosity. Witness: the Gentile collection for Jerusalem showed one family across ethnic lines, and those who received it would glorify God (2 Cor 9:12-13).

items.title: Leading and administration
items.summary: Guiding a community with care and diligence; the Greek word in 1 Cor 12:28 pictures a ship's pilot.
items.detail: Expression: ordering a community so that others can flourish. Witness: when the apostles organised fair food distribution, 'the word of God continued to increase' (Acts 6:1-7).

items.title: Mercy
items.summary: Caring for the suffering, sick and poor, done 'with cheerfulness' (Rom 12:8).
items.detail: Expression: it mirrors the mercy of God. Witness: early Christian care for the sick in plagues impressed even critics. Mercy should not be withheld from those who will never believe (Luke 6:35-36).

items.title: Service and helps
items.summary: Practical, often unseen work that keeps the body functioning.
items.detail: 'Helps' in 1 Cor 12:28 appears only there. Expression: humble love like Jesus washing feet (John 13:14-15). Witness: Peter says those who serve should do so in God's strength 'so that in everything God may be glorified' (1 Pet 4:11).

items.title: Hospitality
items.summary: Welcoming strangers and believers into one's home and table.
items.detail: Peter links hospitality directly to using gifts (1 Pet 4:9-10). Expression: the warmth of God's welcome. Witness: Lydia's house became the base of the church in Philippi (Acts 16:14-15, Acts 16:40).

items.title: Word of wisdom and knowledge
items.summary: Spirit-given insight for a situation or understanding of God's ways.
items.detail: Interpreters differ on whether these are revelatory or wise teaching. Expression: helping people see clearly. Witness: Jesus promised the Spirit would give words to believers on trial before rulers (Luke 21:14-15).

items.title: Faith
items.summary: Unusual trust in God for a particular task or need.
items.detail: Different from the saving faith every believer has. Expression: it encourages a whole community to trust God. Witness: answered prayer and courage in hardship make people ask where the hope comes from.

items.title: Healing and miracles
items.summary: God's power to heal and do signs through believers.
items.detail: Continuationists and cessationists disagree about whether these continue (see /debates/cessationism). Expression: compassion; Jesus healed because he was moved with pity (Mark 1:41). Witness: signs drew attention to the message in Acts (Acts 3:6-16), but Jesus also healed many who did not follow him.

items.title: Discerning spirits
items.summary: Telling the difference between what comes from God and what does not.
items.detail: Expression: protecting people out of love. Witness: a church that is not easily deceived is a safer place for seekers (1 John 4:1).

items.title: Tongues and interpretation
items.summary: Speaking in languages not learned, with interpretation for the church.
items.detail: Paul values tongues for private prayer but asks for interpretation in church so that others are built up (1 Cor 14:2-5). Expression: prayer beyond words. Witness: at Pentecost hearers heard God's works in their own languages (Acts 2:5-11), but Paul warns that uninterpreted tongues may confuse outsiders (1 Cor 14:23).

items.title: Evangelist
items.summary: A particular gift for announcing the gospel and leading people to faith.
items.detail: Not every believer has this gift (Eph 4:11), though all can witness. Expression: joy in good news and love for people. Witness: this is its direct purpose, and the church should honour and support those who have it.

items.title: Apostle and church-planter
items.summary: Sent to start and establish churches where Christ is not known.
items.detail: Whether 'apostle' continues as a role is debated; many use it loosely for pioneer mission. Expression: obedience and love for the unreached. Witness: Paul's ambition was to preach where Christ had not been named (Rom 15:20).

items.title: Shepherding (pastoring)
items.summary: Caring for a flock: feeding, guarding and seeking the lost.
items.detail: Expression: the care of the Good Shepherd (John 10:11). Witness: shepherds are to be examples to the flock (1 Pet 5:2-3) and well thought of by outsiders (1 Tim 3:7).

items.title: Craftsmanship
items.summary: Skill in metal, wood, stone and design, given by the Spirit.
items.detail: Bezalel is the first person 'filled with the Spirit of God' (Exod 31:3). Expression: making beautiful, durable things in the image of the Maker. Witness: Solomon's temple, made with the skill of Hiram of Tyre, drew the nations' attention to Israel's God (1 Kgs 8:41-43).

items.title: Weaving, sewing and textile arts
items.summary: Skilled women spun and wove for the tabernacle; Dorcas sewed for widows.
items.detail: Exodus calls the women who spun 'wise-hearted' (Exod 35:25-26). Expression: care made visible in cloth. Witness: Dorcas' garments were shown with tears when she died, and after she was raised 'many believed in the Lord' (Acts 9:39-42).

items.title: Music
items.summary: Playing and singing with skill, for God and for people.
items.detail: David's playing brought relief to Saul (1 Sam 16:23), and trained musicians led temple worship (1 Chr 25:7). Expression: lament, joy and praise. Witness: Paul and Silas singing in prison were heard by the other prisoners (Acts 16:25), and the Psalms call the nations to sing (Ps 96:1-3).

items.title: Poetry and song-writing
items.summary: Shaping language with beauty and depth.
items.detail: About a third of the Old Testament is poetry. Expression: Ps 45:1 pictures a heart overflowing with a good theme and a tongue like the pen of a ready writer. Witness: poems and hymns teach and carry the faith across generations (Col 3:16).

items.title: Visual art and design
items.summary: Colour, form and pattern for glory and beauty.
items.detail: The priests' garments were to be made 'for glory and for beauty' (Exod 28:2) with pomegranates and gold bells. Expression: beauty that needs no extra justification. Witness: beauty can awaken longing for God that argument alone does not reach.

items.title: Building and engineering
items.summary: Planning, organising and constructing.
items.detail: Nehemiah rebuilt Jerusalem's walls in 52 days. Expression: securing a city's welfare. Witness: the nations around 'perceived that this work had been accomplished with the help of our God' (Neh 6:15-16).

items.title: Farming and care of land
items.summary: Working and keeping the earth to feed others.
items.detail: Isaiah says God himself instructs the farmer in when to plough and how to thresh (Isa 28:23-29). Expression: obedience to the first command to work and keep the garden. Witness: Ruth and Boaz's harvest field becomes a place of kindness and covenant loyalty (Ruth 2:8-12).
people: Uzziah, who loved the soil (2 Chr 26:10)

items.title: Administration and statecraft
items.summary: Running organisations and nations wisely and honestly.
items.detail: Joseph managed Egypt's grain; Daniel served foreign kings so faithfully that his enemies could find no fault (Dan 6:4). Expression: justice and order for the common good. Witness: Pharaoh recognised the Spirit of God in Joseph (Gen 41:38), and Darius praised Daniel's God (Dan 6:25-27).

items.title: Trade and business
items.summary: Producing and selling goods honestly to meet needs.
items.detail: Lydia sold purple cloth; the capable woman of Proverbs 31 buys a field and sells garments. Expression: creativity, provision and generosity (Prov 31:20). Witness: Lydia's business network and home became the first church in Europe (Acts 16:14-15).

items.title: Manual trades that fund mission
items.summary: Working with one's hands to avoid being a burden.
items.detail: Paul worked as a tentmaker or leatherworker (Acts 18:3). Expression: dignity of ordinary labour and love that refuses to burden others. Witness: Paul presented his work as an example of the gospel's freely given grace (1 Thess 2:9, Acts 20:34-35).

items.title: Learning and science
items.summary: Studying God's world and human wisdom.
items.detail: Solomon spoke of trees, animals, birds and fish (1 Kgs 4:33); Daniel and his friends were given skill in all learning (Dan 1:17). Expression: delight in God's works (Ps 111:2). Witness: kings came to hear Solomon's wisdom (1 Kgs 4:34).

items.title: Medicine and care of the body
items.summary: Healing through skill and knowledge.
items.detail: Paul calls Luke 'the beloved physician' (Col 4:14). Expression: honouring the body God made. Witness: Christian hospitals and medical missions have carried both compassion and the gospel, at best without making care conditional on belief.

items.title: Writing and research
items.summary: Careful investigation and orderly writing.
items.detail: Luke 'carefully investigated everything' to write an orderly account (Luke 1:1-4). Expression: love of truth. Witness: his purpose was that Theophilus might know the certainty of what he had been taught.

items.title: Speaking and persuasion
items.summary: Eloquence and the ability to reason in public.
items.detail: Apollos was eloquent and competent in the Scriptures, and he 'powerfully refuted' opponents in public (Acts 18:24-28). Expression: love for clear truth. Witness: direct. Paul also warns against trusting eloquence rather than the cross (1 Cor 2:1-5).

items.title: Dance and bodily celebration
items.summary: Joy expressed with the whole body.
items.detail: Miriam led women with tambourines and dancing after the sea crossing (Exod 15:20-21); David danced before the LORD with all his might (2 Sam 6:14). Expression: whole-body praise. Witness: public celebration showed what God had done, though Michal despised it (2 Sam 6:16).

items.title: Nurture and passing on faith
items.summary: Raising and teaching children in daily life.
items.detail: Israel was to teach God's words at home, on the road, lying down and rising (Deut 6:6-7). Expression: love that shapes a life. Witness: Timothy's faith came first through his grandmother Lois and mother Eunice (2 Tim 1:5).

items.title: Naming, ordering and caring
items.summary: Bringing understanding and order to the created world.
items.detail: Adam's first task after work in the garden is to name the animals (Gen 2:19-20). Expression: sharing God's ordering of chaos in Genesis 1. Witness: when humans rule as caring stewards, creation itself shows the character of its King (Ps 8:3-9).

rows.label: Main purpose
cells: To bring people to faith in Christ; a gift is valuable as a means to evangelism.
To reflect God's image, love neighbours and honour God; a gift is good in itself.
Both: gifts glorify God and serve people in themselves, and that faithful work also witnesses and opens doors for the gospel.

rows.label: Measure of success
cells: Conversations started, decisions made, people reached.
Faithfulness, skill, beauty, truth and real benefit to others.
Faithfulness and love first; fruitfulness in witness is hoped for but left to God (1 Cor 3:6-7).

rows.label: Typical example
cells: A concert with an altar call; a café run mainly to reach customers; a novel written to carry a gospel message.
A Christian composer writing an honest symphony; a nurse caring well without mentioning faith.
A well-run business with fair wages whose owner prays for customers and speaks of Christ when trust allows.

rows.label: Strengths
cells: Takes eternity seriously; keeps the church from forgetting to speak; channels great energy into mission.
Honours creation and craft; frees believers from guilt; treats people as neighbours, not targets.
Holds together creation and redemption, word and deed; fits the whole Bible's story.

rows.label: Risks
cells: Sacred/secular split; art as propaganda; people as projects; burnout and guilt; weak craft.
Silence about Christ; witness becomes vague; comfort with the world as it is; neglect of the lost.
Can become vague 'both/and' that never prioritises; each side may suspect it dilutes their concern.

rows.label: Who holds it
cells: Many revivalists and mass evangelists; some mission agencies; popular youth and church culture.
Many artists and craftspeople; Catholic and Orthodox traditions of beauty; some Kuyperian voices; Jewish teaching on avodah.
Lausanne movement, John Stott, Tim Keller, Andy Crouch, Makoto Fujimura, Dorothy Sayers, Francis Schaeffer.

spectrum.title: What are gifts for?
spectrum.intro: These are real positions held by sincere Christians. Most do not deny the other pole entirely; they differ on emphasis and priority. Place yourself, then read the position on the other side as its best defenders would put it.
spectrum.right: Mainly expression of the image of God and love of neighbour

stops.label: Revivalist urgency
stops.text: The world is a sinking ship and time is short. Every gift, from singing to business, should be harnessed to rescue souls. This view grew from real love and urgency and fuelled great missionary sacrifice.
stops.who: Many nineteenth- and twentieth-century revivalists (Finney, Moody); parts of mass-evangelism culture

stops.label: Great Commission priority
stops.text: Christians should do good works and honour God in their jobs, but the church's unique mission is making disciples. Because eternal destinies are at stake, proclamation has priority, and this should shape how gifts are directed.
stops.who: Kevin DeYoung and Greg Gilbert; John Piper (with his stress that worship, not missions, is the ultimate goal); many Great-Commission-focused evangelicals

stops.label: Holistic mission with evangelism primary
stops.text: Evangelism and social responsibility are both Christian duty and belong together, like two wings, but in the church's mission evangelism is primary. Gifts serve both word and deed.
stops.who: Lausanne Covenant (1974); John Stott; the Grand Rapids report (1982)

stops.label: Integral mission and faith-work
stops.text: Word and deed are inseparable parts of one mission. Ordinary work is a calling, and the sacred/secular divide must go. Witness flows from integrated lives rather than from added messages.
stops.who: Latin American theologians René Padilla and Samuel Escobar; Tim Keller; Andy Crouch; the Cape Town Commitment (2010)

stops.label: Anabaptist community witness
stops.text: Gifts are first for building a visible community that lives the way of Jesus: sharing, peacemaking, simple living. The church's life together is its witness, more than individual achievement or cultural influence.
stops.who: Mennonite and Anabaptist traditions; John Howard Yoder; Stanley Hauerwas (influenced by this tradition)

stops.label: Kuyperian cultural calling
stops.text: Christ claims every square inch of life. Science, art, politics and business are callings in their own right, with their own God-given standards, not merely platforms for evangelism.
stops.who: Abraham Kuyper; Herman Bavinck; Hans Rookmaaker; Al Wolters; Richard Mouw; Francis Schaeffer (in his writing on art)

stops.label: Sacramental beauty
stops.text: Beauty, liturgy, icons and craft can make God's presence and goodness visible. Art serves worship and the human person; it is not reducible to a message.
stops.who: Catholic tradition (John Paul II, *Letter to Artists*, 1999); Orthodox iconography and liturgy; Anglican and high-church traditions

stops.label: Art as gift, not weapon
stops.text: The artist offers beauty gratuitously, as God made the world, and tends culture like a garden. Making art only to win arguments damages both the art and the gospel.
stops.who: Makoto Fujimura; Dorothy L. Sayers; J. R. R. Tolkien's idea of 'sub-creation'; many Christian artists

cases.title: Bezalel and Oholiab: Spirit-filled artists
cases.question: What does it mean that the first person 'filled with the Spirit' is a craftsman?

steps.note: God calls Bezalel 'by name' and fills him with the Spirit of God, with wisdom, understanding, knowledge and all craftsmanship (Exod 31:2-3). The language matches the way the Spirit equips prophets and kings.

The tabernacle, its furniture, the priests' garments 'for glory and for beauty' (Exod 28:2). Their work is for worship, but much of it is ornament: almond blossoms, pomegranates, cherubim. Beauty is part of the purpose.
God also gives them the ability to teach others (Exod 35:34). Gifts are passed on in community, and many 'wise-hearted' men and women join the work (Exod 36:1-2).

Straight after the call comes the Sabbath command (Exod 31:12-17). Later Jewish teaching derived the categories of work forbidden on the Sabbath from the labours of building the tabernacle (Talmud, Shabbat 49b). Holy work is good, and it still stops for rest.

cases.takeaway: Artistic skill can be a direct gift of the Spirit, given for worship and beauty, taught in community and bounded by rest. It did not need to 'lead to evangelism' to be holy.

cases.title: David's harp for Saul
cases.question: Is it ministry when a gifted person simply helps someone who suffers?

steps.note: Saul is tormented by a harmful spirit, and his servants look for 'a man who is skilful in playing the lyre' (1 Sam 16:16).
He is skilful in playing, a man of valour, prudent in speech, of good presence, 'and the LORD is with him' (1 Sam 16:18). Skill and godliness are named together.
When David plays, Saul is refreshed and the harmful spirit departs (1 Sam 16:23). There is no sermon; the music itself is the service.
The same gift later produces psalms that Israel sang for centuries. David's music served one troubled king and also became a witness to the nations (Ps 57:9).

cases.takeaway: A skill used with care for one suffering person is real service to God. Over time, such faithfulness can become a far wider witness than anyone planned.

cases.title: Dorcas and her sewing
cases.question: How does practical craft become both love and witness?

steps.note: Luke calls Tabitha (Dorcas) a disciple 'full of good works and acts of charity' (Acts 9:36). Her name is given in both Aramaic and Greek, which may suggest she moved in both communities.
At her death the widows weep and show Peter the tunics and garments she made while she was with them (Acts 9:39). Her love was stitched into clothing for the poor.

Peter prays and she is raised, and it 'became known throughout all Joppa, and many believed in the Lord' (Acts 9:42). Strictly, the miracle led to faith; but it was her life of love that drew the grieving community together.
The text does not say she sewed in order to evangelise. It presents her work as good in itself, and God used it within a larger witness.

cases.takeaway: Ordinary craft offered in love is honoured by God and remembered by the church; witness grew around a life of mercy rather than replacing it.

cases.title: Paul the tentmaker
cases.question: Was Paul's trade only a way to fund 'real' ministry?

steps.note: Paul stays with Aquila and Priscilla in Corinth 'because he was of the same trade', working as tentmakers (Acts 18:3). The Greek word may mean leatherworker; scholars debate the details.

He worked night and day so as not to burden anyone while preaching (1 Thess 2:9), and to give an example of honest work to idle believers (2 Thess 3:7-9). He also gave up his right to support so the gospel would be free of charge (1 Cor 9:12-18).

steps.step: The workshop as a place of witness
steps.note: Ancient workshops were places of conversation. Many scholars (for example Ronald Hock) suggest Paul's workshop was itself a setting for teaching.

Paul did value his work partly for the gospel's sake. Yet he also told ordinary believers to work quietly with their hands to win the respect of outsiders and depend on no one (1 Thess 4:11-12), and to work so they could share with those in need (Eph 4:28).

cases.takeaway: Paul shows the integrated view: honest manual work has dignity, supports others and also serves the gospel. Both instrument and expression are present, and neither cancels the other.

cases.title: The woman's perfume: 'a beautiful thing'
cases.question: What does Jesus say about an extravagant gift with no practical use?

steps.note: A woman breaks a jar of costly nard, worth about a year's wages, and pours it on Jesus' head (Mark 14:3-5).
Some say it should have been sold and given to the poor. Their logic is efficiency: a gift is valued by its usefulness.
'She has done a beautiful thing to me' (Mark 14:6). The Greek kalon ergon means a good or beautiful work. Jesus defends an act of pure devotion and links it to his coming burial (Mark 14:8).

Jesus says that wherever the gospel is proclaimed in the whole world, what she has done will be told in memory of her (Mark 14:9). An act with no evangelistic purpose became part of the gospel's own proclamation.

cases.takeaway: Worship and beauty offered to Jesus need no further justification, and God may weave such expression into the gospel's witness far beyond our planning.

cases.title: Daniel's administrative excellence
cases.question: How does faithful work in a non-Christian setting honour God?

steps.note: Daniel serves Babylonian and Persian kings as an exile. Jeremiah had told exiles to seek the welfare of the city and pray for it (Jer 29:7).
He distinguishes himself because 'an excellent spirit was in him', and the king plans to set him over the whole kingdom (Dan 6:3). His rivals can find no corruption or negligence (Dan 6:4).
The only charge they can bring concerns his God. He keeps praying three times a day toward Jerusalem (Dan 6:10).
After the lions' den, Darius writes to all peoples that they should fear the God of Daniel (Dan 6:25-27). Daniel's witness rested on years of competent, honest work and visible devotion.

cases.takeaway: Competent, honest service in a secular workplace is itself faithfulness to God, and combined with open devotion it can become a public witness.

sections.heading: The image of God and human creativity
sections.body:
The Bible begins with God as maker. He speaks, separates, forms, fills and calls things good (Gen 1:31). Then he makes humans 'in his image' and tells them to fill and rule the earth (Gen 1:26-28). Whatever else the image of God means, in context it includes representing God and sharing, in a creaturely way, in his creative and ordering work. Adam is put in the garden 'to work it and keep it' (Gen 2:15) and names the animals (Gen 2:19-20).

This means human creativity is not a distraction from spiritual life. It is part of being human. When a carpenter makes a sound chair, a scientist names a new species, or a mother turns a house into a home, they are doing a small version of what God did in Genesis 1: bringing order, beauty and life.

Theologians call this the 'cultural mandate': the calling to develop the world's possibilities. Dorothy Sayers, in *The Mind of the Maker* (1941), argued that the one thing we are told about God before we are told we are made in his image is that he creates. J. R. R. Tolkien called human art 'sub-creation': we make because we are made by a Maker.

Sin damages this calling. Work becomes toil (Gen 3:17-19), and the first city and the first metalworker appear in Cain's line (Gen 4:17-22). Yet God does not withdraw the gift. Culture remains good and also corrupted, waiting for redemption.

callout.text: Scholars debate what the 'image of God' is: a capacity (reason, creativity), a relationship (with God and others), or a royal function (representing God's rule). Most now stress the functional and relational readings. All three support seeing creativity as part of human dignity.

sections.heading: Talents and spiritual gifts: what the words mean
sections.body:
In Jesus' parable, a 'talent' (Greek talanton) was a unit of weight for silver or gold. One talent was worth roughly 6,000 denarii, about twenty years' wages for a labourer. The servants receive money 'each according to his ability' (Matt 25:15). The parable is about faithfulness with what the master entrusts while he is away, and about the coming judgement.

The English meaning of 'talent' as a natural ability grew from medieval and later Christian readings of this parable. So when preachers apply the parable to musical or athletic talent, they are making an application, not giving the original meaning. That application is not wrong in itself, since stewardship covers everything God entrusts (1 Pet 4:10), but the first audience would have heard something different. Some scholars (for example Joachim Jeremias) think the parable first targeted leaders who buried God's gift to Israel instead of sharing it.

'Spiritual gifts' translates charismata, from charis, grace. In the New Testament it covers prophecy and tongues, but also giving, leading and showing mercy (Rom 12:6-8). Peter speaks of 'God's varied grace' in two broad kinds: speaking and serving (1 Pet 4:10-11).

The Old Testament blurs the line further. Bezalel's craft is a gift of the Spirit (Exod 31:3), and Isaiah says the farmer's wisdom comes from God (Isa 28:26). Many teachers therefore say that the difference between 'natural talents' and 'spiritual gifts' is less sharp than we often think: both are God's gifts, both are to serve others, and the Spirit can take up and transform natural ability.

callout.text: Myth: the parable of the talents is about natural abilities. In the story a talent is money. Applying it to abilities is a later, legitimate extension, but it is not the parable's original subject.

sections.heading: Spirit gifts: love and building up the body
sections.body:
Paul's longest discussion of gifts (1 Corinthians 12-14) was written to a church that ranked people by spectacular abilities. His answer has three movements. First, all gifts come from the same Spirit, Lord and God and are given 'for the common good' (1 Cor 12:4-7). Second, the church is a body: the eye cannot say to the hand 'I have no need of you', and the parts that seem weaker are indispensable (1 Cor 12:21-22). Third, without love every gift is worthless (1 Cor 13:1-3).

In chapter 14 Paul gives a practical test: does this build up the church? He prefers prophecy to uninterpreted tongues in the meeting because it builds others up (1 Cor 14:3-5), and he says 'let all things be done for building up' (1 Cor 14:26).

So the main purpose Paul gives for Spirit gifts is not evangelism as such but love and the building up of the body. Yet the two connect. Paul imagines an outsider coming into a meeting and being convicted by prophecy, so that he falls down and worships God (1 Cor 14:24-25). Jesus said that the disciples' love for one another would show the world they belong to him (John 13:35). A loving, healthy church is itself a witness.

This is also where the existing gift lists in the app can mislead if read alone. Paul places the fruit of love above all gifts (Gal 5:22-23, 1 Cor 13:13).

sections.heading: Work and vocation: serving God in ordinary life
sections.body:
Paul tells believers, including slaves in harsh households, 'Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men' (Col 3:23-24). He tells the Thessalonians to work with their hands and live quietly (1 Thess 4:11-12), and he tells former thieves to work so they can share with those in need (Eph 4:28). Work is service to God, provision for oneself and a way to love others.

For much of church history, however, a two-level view dominated. Eusebius of Caesarea (early fourth century) described a 'perfect' life of prayer and renunciation and a 'permitted' life of farming, trade and family. In the medieval West, 'vocation' usually meant a call to the priesthood or religious orders.

Martin Luther challenged this. In his 1520 writings he argued that all baptised believers are priests and that the work of a farmer or housemaid is no less holy than that of a monk. He taught that God cares for the world through ordinary callings, which he called 'masks of God'. Calvin added that each calling is like a 'sentry post' assigned by God (*Institutes* 3.10.6). The Puritans spoke of a 'general calling' to follow Christ and 'particular callings' to trades.

Two popular quotations need care. The line 'God milks the cows through the vocation of the milkmaid' is a fair summary of Luther's idea but is usually traced to Gustaf Wingren's book *Luther on Vocation*, not to a confirmed Luther sentence. The line about the Christian shoemaker making good shoes rather than putting little crosses on them is widely attributed to Luther but has no known source in his writings; scholars such as Frederick Gaiser think it is a modern saying.

callout.text: Myth: Luther said 'The Christian shoemaker does his duty not by putting little crosses on the shoes, but by making good shoes.' No source in Luther's works is known. It summarises his view well enough, but it should not be quoted as his words.

sections.heading: Why evangelicals turned gifts into tools for evangelism
sections.body:
To understand this framing, start with its best motives. Evangelicals believe that people without Christ face real, eternal loss and that the gospel is God's power to save (Rom 1:16). Jesus commanded his followers to make disciples of all nations (Matt 28:18-20), and Paul asked how people can believe without hearing (Rom 10:14). If that is true, then love itself seems to require urgency. Many who 'used every gift for the gospel' gave up comfort, careers and even their lives out of love for people they had never met.

History sharpened this instinct. The revivals of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries made conversion the central Christian event. Charles Finney taught that revival came through the right use of means, so techniques and music were enlisted. D. L. Moody pictured the world as a wrecked ship and his calling as saving as many as possible in a lifeboat. Ira Sankey's songs were written to prepare hearts for the sermon. Premillennial expectation, the belief that Christ would soon return and the world would grow worse before then, made improving culture seem like 'polishing brass on a sinking ship'.

In the early twentieth century the Fundamentalist-Modernist conflict hardened this. Liberal Protestants stressed the 'social gospel' and cultural progress; many conservatives responded by focusing almost entirely on personal salvation. Historian Timothy L. Smith and sociologist David Moberg (*The Great Reversal*, 1972) called this retreat from social and cultural engagement the 'great reversal', since nineteenth-century evangelicals had been deeply involved in reform.

From this came familiar patterns: the saying that 'only two things last forever, God's word and people's souls'; tracts left with restaurant tips; concerts and sports events valued mainly for the altar call; and a market in 'Christian' products, from music to mints, defined by explicit religious content. Many sincere believers learned to ask of every activity, 'How can I use this to share the gospel?'

callout.text: Read this history charitably. The evangelistic framing grew from love, from obedience to Christ's command and from a sincere view of eternity. Critics who forget this tend to caricature it.

sections.heading: The costs of making every gift a tool
sections.body:
Even its friends now admit the instrumental view has had real costs.

First, a sacred/secular divide. If only evangelism and church work truly count, most Christians spend most of their week on things they believe God does not much care about. The Lausanne Cape Town Commitment (2010) named this divide as one of the greatest obstacles to mobilising God's people for mission.

Second, art as propaganda. Francis Schaeffer warned in *Art and the Bible* (1973) that a Christian's art does not need to be justified by being a vehicle for evangelism. When songs must contain enough 'Jesus' references to count, or stories exist only to carry a message, the craft often becomes weak and the message hollow. Outsiders recognise advertising.

Third, people as projects. When a friendship is valued only as a route to conversion, people feel it. Jesus' love did not depend on response: he healed ten lepers when only one came back (Luke 17:11-19).

Fourth, burnout and guilt. Believers who think their job is spiritually worthless may either overload church activity or quietly despair. Sayers argued that the church lost the working world partly because it showed no interest in whether their work was good.

Fifth, a smaller gospel. If God cares only about souls, the Bible's hope of resurrection bodies and a renewed creation (Rom 8:19-23) shrinks into an escape from the world.

callout.text: Defenders reply that these are abuses, not the view itself. Careful Great-Commission evangelicals also affirm vocation and beauty; they insist only that the eternal stakes give proclamation a special priority.

sections.heading: The best evangelical responses, and the strongest defence of priority
sections.body:
Within evangelicalism itself a rich response developed. Carl Henry's *The Uneasy Conscience of Modern Fundamentalism* (1947) urged conservatives to re-engage society. The Lausanne Covenant (1974), drafted largely by John Stott, affirmed that evangelism and social responsibility are both part of Christian duty, while also saying that evangelism is primary in the church's mission of sacrificial service. Stott liked to describe word and deed as partners. Later voices went further: René Padilla and Samuel Escobar spoke of 'integral mission'; Tim Keller (*Every Good Endeavor*, 2012) taught that work is part of God's design; Andy Crouch (*Culture Making*, 2008) argued that Christians should create good culture, not only condemn or copy it; Makoto Fujimura calls for 'culture care'.

The strongest defence of evangelistic priority deserves equal hearing. Kevin DeYoung and Greg Gilbert (*What Is the Mission of the Church?*, 2011) argue that the church as an institution has a specific mission, given in the Great Commission: to make disciples by proclaiming the gospel and teaching obedience. They warn that if 'mission' means everything good, it soon means nothing, and the hardest task, telling people about Christ, quietly drops away. Importantly, they do not deny that individual Christians honour God in their vocations; they affirm it.

John Piper adds a different angle: 'Missions exists because worship doesn't' (*Let the Nations Be Glad*, 1993). Worship of God is the ultimate goal; evangelism serves it. This actually supports valuing gifts as worship, while keeping urgency for those who do not yet worship.

The honest conclusion is that both sides agree on more than they often think: proclamation is necessary, good work matters to God, and love must drive both. Their real disagreement is over the church's priorities and how 'mission' should be defined.

sections.heading: The Jewish relational lens: avodah, Sabbath and the world as gift
sections.body:
The Hebrew root avad stands behind words for work, service and worship. Adam is to work (avad) the ground (Gen 2:15). God tells Moses that Israel will serve (avad) him at Sinai (Exod 3:12). The Ten Commandments say 'six days you shall labour' with the same root (Exod 20:9). Later, avodah became the name for the temple service, and after the temple fell, the rabbis called prayer 'the service of the heart'. The language itself suggests that work and worship are not two separate worlds.

The Sabbath sets a boundary on work. Six days of labour are commanded, and so is the seventh day of rest (Exod 20:8-11). Deuteronomy grounds it in freedom from slavery (Deut 5:12-15): a people who rest show they are no longer defined by output. The rabbis derived the 39 categories of work forbidden on the Sabbath from the tasks used in building the tabernacle (Talmud, Shabbat 49b), so the very work of Bezalel defines what rest means.

Jewish tradition also treats the world as a gift that calls for thanks. The Talmud says that enjoying anything in this world without a blessing is like taking what belongs to God (Berakhot 35a). Blessings are said over bread, fruit, a rainbow and even new clothes. Everyday enjoyment becomes relationship with the Giver.

Be careful with the popular phrase tikkun olam, 'repairing the world'. In the Mishnah it refers to legal rulings made 'for the good order of the world'. The Aleinu prayer hopes 'to perfect the world under the kingdom of the Almighty'. Lurianic Kabbalah (sixteenth century) gave it a cosmic, mystical meaning, and modern Jewish movements use it for social action. It should not be presented as a single ancient doctrine that human work fixes the world.

For Christians this lens helps: gifts are received within a covenant relationship, used in service that is also worship, and held lightly by people who rest.

callout.text: Rabbinic sources cited here (Shabbat 49b, Berakhot 35a) are later than the Bible and belong to Jewish tradition. They show how Jewish readers have understood these texts, not what the biblical authors stated.

sections.heading: A healthy integrated vision
sections.body:
Putting this together, a gift is first a grace received (1 Cor 4:7). It reflects the creativity of the God whose image we bear. It is meant to be developed with skill, offered in love, and used to serve the church and our neighbours. Done this way, it is worship (Rom 12:1).

Witness is not an extra layer stuck on top. It grows naturally from faithful, excellent, loving work, as Jesus said: people see good works and glorify the Father (Matt 5:16). And because people need to hear the good news, Christians should also be ready to speak, with gentleness and respect (1 Pet 3:15). Expression and witness are partners.

The final hope matters here. Paul ends his resurrection chapter by saying that labour in the Lord is not in vain (1 Cor 15:58). Revelation pictures the glory and honour of the nations brought into the new Jerusalem (Rev 21:24-26). Interpreters differ on how literally to take this, but it suggests that what is good and true in human culture is not simply thrown away. Our work, tested and purified, may in some way last (1 Cor 3:12-14).

Practically: do your work well; love the people it serves; pray for them; speak of Christ when trust and opportunity allow; rest; and give thanks. Do not despise the gifted evangelist, and do not despise the gifted carpenter. Both belong to one body.

misreadings.topic: The parable of the talents is about natural abilities
misreadings.popular: God gives each person natural talents, such as music, sport or business, and will judge whether we used them for him. Burying your talent means wasting your abilities.
misreadings.inContext: A talent was a large sum of money, and the servants receive it 'each according to his ability' (Matt 25:15), so ability and the entrusted gift are distinct. In Matthew the parable sits among warnings about readiness for the Son of Man's return (Matt 24-25). Many scholars (Joachim Jeremias, and more recently R. T. France) see the entrusted wealth as the kingdom, God's word or the responsibilities given to disciples; Jeremias thought it first targeted leaders who 'buried' God's gift to Israel. The English sense of 'talent' as ability comes from later readings of this parable.
misreadings.defence: Traditional evangelical commentators (for example D. A. Carson and Craig Blomberg) agree on the money detail, but note that the principle of faithful stewardship applies to all God entrusts, including abilities (1 Pet 4:10). Applying the parable to talents is a legitimate extension, provided we do not miss its main point: active faithfulness while awaiting the master's return.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Reading it only as 'use your abilities' can turn it into a productivity lesson. Reading it in context keeps the focus on faithfulness to the Master, which covers abilities but is bigger than them.

misreadings.topic: 'Do all to the glory of God' means everything must point people to Christ
misreadings.popular: 1 Cor 10:31 means that every activity, even eating and drinking, should be done in a way that explicitly points people to Jesus and opens a door for the gospel.
misreadings.inContext: The verse concludes Paul's long discussion of food offered to idols (1 Cor 8-10). Glorifying God here means acting with thanksgiving (1 Cor 10:30), avoiding idolatry and not harming a weaker believer's conscience. Ordinary eating, received with thanks, can glorify God. Scholars such as Gordon Fee and Anthony Thiselton stress this pastoral context.
misreadings.defence: The evangelistic reading has real support in the very next verses: Paul says he tries to please everyone 'not seeking my own advantage, but that of many, that they may be saved' (1 Cor 10:32-33). Careful evangelical readers (for example D. A. Carson and Thomas Schreiner) conclude that glorifying God includes thanksgiving and love, and that concern for others' salvation is part of that love. The popular reading is not wrong, just too narrow.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Both truths free and focus us: ordinary life received with thanks honours God, and our freedom should be used with concern for others' salvation.

misreadings.topic: 'Redeem the time' means fill every moment with spiritual activity
misreadings.popular: Eph 5:16 ('redeeming the time') means believers should not waste time on hobbies, art or leisure, but use every moment for prayer, Bible study and evangelism.
misreadings.inContext: The phrase means 'making the most of the opportunity' (Greek kairos, a fitting moment) 'because the days are evil'. In Col 4:5 the same phrase concerns wise conduct toward outsiders. It is about wisdom and alertness, not about eliminating rest or creativity. Scripture also commands rest and celebrates feasts.
misreadings.defence: Evangelical scholars such as Peter O'Brien and Douglas Moo note that the phrase does carry urgency, especially in Colossians, where it is linked to gracious speech with outsiders (Col 4:5-6). The evangelistic reading is fair for Colossians; the error is turning it into a rule against ordinary enjoyment.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Read as 'never rest', it leads to burnout and guilt. Read as 'live wisely and seize real opportunities', it fits both Sabbath and witness.

misreadings.popular: 'Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord' is often quoted for volunteers in church ministry, as if church work is where we truly serve the Lord.
misreadings.inContext: Paul is addressing slaves working in ordinary households (Col 3:22-25). The most menial labour, done for earthly masters, is service to the Lord Christ who will reward it. The verse is the opposite of a sacred/secular split: it sanctifies everyday work.
misreadings.defence: Few scholars dispute this. Evangelical commentators like Douglas Moo agree it applies to all work. Some note that the verse should not be used to ignore the injustice of slavery; it addresses how believers act within a hard situation, and Paul also commands masters to be just (Col 4:1).
misreadings.whyItMatters: This verse is one of the clearest biblical answers to the guilt many Christians feel about 'secular' jobs.

misreadings.topic: Every gift must be used for evangelism
misreadings.popular: The Great Commission is the church's one task, so a gift that does not lead to sharing the gospel is a wasted gift.
misreadings.inContext: The New Testament gives gifts several purposes: building up the body (1 Cor 14:12), serving others (1 Pet 4:10), glorifying God (1 Pet 4:11) and showing love (1 Cor 13). The Old Testament honours craft, music and wise administration in their own right (Exod 31:1-6, Prov 22:29). Writers such as Tim Keller and Andy Crouch argue that evangelism is essential but is not the only thing God cares about.
misreadings.defence: Great-Commission evangelicals such as Kevin DeYoung and Greg Gilbert answer that they do not claim every gift must be evangelism. Their claim is narrower: the church as an institution has proclamation as its distinct mission, while individual Christians serve God in many ways. They warn that without this priority, evangelism gets crowded out.
misreadings.whyItMatters: The difference is between saying 'evangelism matters most for the church's mission' and 'nothing else matters'. The first is a serious position; the second is a popular distortion.

misreadings.popular: Only two things last forever: God's word and people's souls. So the only work with eternal value is work that saves souls.
misreadings.inContext: The Bible's hope is bodily resurrection and a renewed creation (Rom 8:19-23, Rev 21:1-5), not only souls in heaven. Revelation pictures the glory of the nations entering the city (Rev 21:24-26), and Paul says labour in the Lord is not in vain (1 Cor 15:58). N. T. Wright and Richard Middleton argue that good work done now is somehow taken up into God's new creation.
misreadings.defence: Many evangelicals (for example Douglas Moo on 2 Peter) note that 2 Pet 3:10-12 speaks of the present world being dissolved by fire, so the continuity of human works is uncertain. They agree that persons, not projects, are what we can be sure will last, and that this should give evangelism urgency. Both sides agree the saying is too simple: God's word and people last, and resurrection means more than souls.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Your view of what lasts shapes whether you value craft, care and culture as part of God's purposes or treat them as disposable.

misreadings.topic: Spiritual gifts are supernatural; talents are merely natural
misreadings.popular: Spiritual gifts are special abilities the Spirit gives at conversion; natural talents are human abilities and are less spiritual.
misreadings.inContext: Bezalel's craft is called the work of the Spirit (Exod 31:3), Isaiah says God teaches the farmer (Isa 28:26), and Paul lists ordinary activities like giving and leading among the charismata (Rom 12:8). Many scholars (for example Gordon Fee, James Dunn) stress that in Paul a 'charisma' is any concrete expression of grace for others.
misreadings.defence: Some evangelicals rightly answer that the New Testament does distinguish the Spirit's gifts within the church, given for its building up, from abilities everyone has by common grace. Being a good musician does not make someone a worship leader. The gifts are related but not identical; the Spirit can take up natural ability and direct it to new ends.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Too sharp a split devalues ordinary gifts; too little distinction can forget that the Spirit's gifts are for the church's building up in love.

misreadings.topic: Being seen versus not being seen
misreadings.popular: Jesus said 'let your light shine before others' (Matt 5:16), so Christians should make their good works and gifts visible as advertisements for the faith.
misreadings.inContext: In the same sermon Jesus warns against doing good works 'to be seen' (Matt 6:1-4). The difference is purpose: in Matt 5:16 the aim is that people glorify the Father; in Matt 6 the aim is one's own reputation. Light shines by being light, not by marketing.
misreadings.defence: Evangelical commentators (for example Craig Keener and D. A. Carson) agree there is no contradiction: visible good works are right when they point to God, and wrong when they serve self. The evangelistic instinct to let works be seen is biblical, if the motive is God's glory.
misreadings.whyItMatters: This keeps gifts from becoming either hidden out of false modesty or displayed out of pride.

views.name: Evangelistic priority (Great Commission focus)
views.who: Revivalist tradition; Kevin DeYoung and Greg Gilbert; John Piper; many mission agencies
views.summary: Because people face eternal destinies, proclaiming Christ has a unique urgency. The church's distinct mission is to make disciples. Christians should do good work, but the church must not let other good things crowd out evangelism.
views.strengths: Takes eternity and the Great Commission seriously; guards against the loss of evangelism seen in some mainline churches; has inspired great sacrifice and missionary love.
views.critiques: At popular level it can create a sacred/secular split, art as propaganda and people as projects. Critics say it can shrink the Bible's story to rescue from the world rather than renewal of it.

views.name: Holistic mission (Lausanne)
views.who: Lausanne Covenant (1974); John Stott; Grand Rapids report (1982); Chris Wright
views.summary: Evangelism and social responsibility are both Christian duty and partners in mission. Evangelism has a certain primacy, but word and deed go together.
views.strengths: Holds together Scripture's concern for proclamation and for justice and mercy; broad support across global evangelicalism.
views.critiques: Some say 'primacy' still keeps culture and work second-class; others say 'holistic' can blur the church's distinct task and let evangelism fade.

views.name: Integral mission and faith-work
views.who: René Padilla; Samuel Escobar; Tim Keller; Katherine Leary Alsdorf; Andy Crouch; the Cape Town Commitment (2010)
views.summary: Word and deed are inseparable parts of one mission. Ordinary work is a calling, the sacred/secular divide must be rejected, and witness flows from integrated lives.
views.strengths: Gives dignity to ordinary Christians' weekday lives; fits Col 3:23 and the Reformation doctrine of vocation; produces better craft and more natural witness.
views.critiques: DeYoung and Gilbert warn that when everything is mission, nothing is; critics also say faith-work talk can drift toward a professional-class focus that neglects manual and low-paid workers.

views.name: Neo-Calvinist cultural calling
views.who: Abraham Kuyper; Herman Bavinck; Hans Rookmaaker; Al Wolters; Richard Mouw; Francis Schaeffer on art
views.summary: Christ is Lord of every area of life. Each sphere, such as art, science, business and politics, has its own God-given norms, and Christians serve God by working faithfully within them.
views.strengths: A strong theology of creation and culture; values art and science on their own terms; hope for a renewed creation.
views.critiques: Can become triumphalist or political; may underplay the call to personal conversion; critics from the Anabaptist side say it trusts cultural power too much.

views.name: Sacramental and beauty traditions
views.who: Catholic tradition (John Paul II, *Letter to Artists*); Eastern Orthodox iconography and liturgy; Anglo-Catholic traditions
views.summary: Beauty and material things can mediate God's presence. Art, music and architecture serve worship and human dignity, and beauty itself draws people to God.
views.strengths: Long experience of art in worship; deep theology of incarnation and creation; witness through beauty that does not reduce art to a message.
views.critiques: Protestants worry about images and ritual replacing the word; some say beauty can become an end in itself or a mark of wealth.

views.name: Anabaptist community witness
views.who: Mennonite and Brethren traditions; John Howard Yoder; Stanley Hauerwas (influenced by it)
views.summary: Gifts serve first to build a visible community of disciples living the way of Jesus. The church's shared life, peacemaking and simplicity are its primary witness.
views.strengths: Takes the church as a body seriously; resists using gifts for status or power; guards against both individualism and cultural compromise.
views.critiques: May undervalue individual vocations in wider society, the arts or public life; critics say it can become withdrawn from culture.

views.name: Art as gift (artists' voices)
views.who: Makoto Fujimura; Dorothy L. Sayers; J. R. R. Tolkien; Madeleine L'Engle
views.summary: Making is part of bearing God's image. Art should be offered as a gift, honestly and well, not used as a weapon or advertisement. Such art witnesses because it is true and beautiful.
views.strengths: Restores dignity to craft; draws from the Bible's own poetry and beauty; often reaches people that direct argument cannot.
views.critiques: May neglect explicit proclamation; can seem elitist or remote from everyday church life; the boundary between 'gift' and self-expression can blur.

practice.title: Gift inventory with community feedback
steps: List what you do well, what you love doing, and what others regularly ask you to help with. Include both 'church' gifts and work, craft and home skills.
Ask three people who know you well (one from church, one from work or school, one from family) what they see as your gifts. Write down their answers without arguing.
Compare the lists. Where do they agree? Where do others see something you do not?
For each gift, write one way it builds up the church and one way it serves people outside the church.
Pray, thanking God by name for each gift (1 Cor 4:7).

practice.title: The Bezalel reading: a small group study
steps: Read Exod 31:1-11, Exod 35:30-36:7 and Exod 39:42-43 aloud.
Note every phrase about skill, wisdom, the Spirit, willing hearts and teaching.
Discuss: Why might God give the first 'filling with the Spirit' to an artist? What does it say about your own work?
Read Exod 31:12-17. Discuss why the Sabbath command comes right after the call to build.
Each person names one piece of work they will do this week 'with skill, for glory and for beauty'.

practice.title: Workplace witness without projects
steps: Write the names of five people you work or study with.
Pray for each by name every day for a month, for their good and not only their conversion.
Ask: how can my work serve them better this week? Do one concrete thing.
Notice natural openings to speak about your hope, and take them gently (1 Pet 3:15). Do not force any.
At the end of the month, reflect: did I treat them as neighbours or as targets?

practice.title: A Sabbath from usefulness
steps: Choose a day or half-day this week to stop productive work.
Do something creative or beautiful with no goal: walk, draw, cook, play music, read poetry.
Say a blessing or prayer of thanks over ordinary things: food, light, people.
Afterwards, write down how it felt to be loved without producing anything.
Read Exod 20:8-11 and Deut 5:12-15 and discuss what freedom the Sabbath gives.

practice.title: Craft and message: an honest review
steps: Pick one piece of 'Christian' art, music or media and one piece of art by a Christian that does not mention faith directly.
Ask of each: Is it true? Is it well made? Is it beautiful? Does it love its audience?
Discuss Schaeffer's claim that art does not need to justify itself as evangelism, and DeYoung and Gilbert's concern that the church not forget to proclaim.
If you make things, choose one thing to improve in your craft this month.
